one_liner: Header-only C99 xor and binary fuse filters: static membership filters with fewer bits/key and faster lookups than Bloom/cuckoo.
what_it_does: Builds an immutable approximate-membership filter from a complete array of distinct 64-bit keys, then answers 'maybe present / definitely absent' queries. The C API is allocate, populate, contain, free (binary_fuse8/16_* and xor8/16_*), plus serialize/deserialize, a packed wire format, and a deserialize_header call that lets fingerprints stay in caller-owned or mmap'd memory. Strings and other types must be hashed to 64 bits first. Keys are re-mixed internally with a Murmur finalizer, so the README says hash quality does not matter beyond avoiding collisions. 8-bit fingerprints give about 0.39% false positives and 16-bit about 0.0015%.
how_it_is_fast: Each key maps to three array slots, and construction stores fingerprints so that the XOR of those three slots equals the key's fingerprint. A query is one hash, three independent memory loads and a compare, with the same cost for hits and misses; a Bloom filter needs up to k probes and slows down when most queried keys are present. Construction is hypergraph peeling: slots touched by exactly one key are removed repeatedly, then assigned in reverse order, retrying with a new seed if peeling stalls. Binary fuse filters (spatially coupled, after Dietzfelbinger and Walzer) keep the three slots in consecutive small segments and pre-bucket hashes by segment, which improves cache locality and shrinks the array from about 1.23n to 1.125n slots. Index reduction uses multiply-shift instead of modulo.
when_to_use: The key set is known up front and read-only: SSTable or segment filters in an LSM/columnar store, leaked-password lists, precomputed deny-lists shipped to clients.
Memory per key matters: binary_fuse8 is about 9 bits/key at 0.39% FPP for sets of 1M keys or more, against 12 bits/key for a Bloom filter at a similar (0.31%) FPP.
Most queried keys are present: xor and fuse lookups always do exactly three loads, while standard Bloom filters get slower on hits (xor paper Fig. 4).
You want a dependency-free file to vendor into C or C++ (nDPI and InfiniFlow Infinity embed binaryfusefilter.h), with serialization and mmap-friendly loading.
You need a very low FPP without a big filter: binary_fuse16 gives about 0.0015% at roughly 18 bits/key.
when_not_to_use: You need inserts, deletes or filter unions: there is no add/remove, and filters built on partitions cannot be OR-ed together the way Bloom filters can (issue #35). Rebuilding needs the full key set.
Lowest query latency matters more than memory: the blocked Bloom filter was faster in both papers (16 ns vs Xor8's 23 ns at 10M keys) at 10.7 bits/key and about 0.94% FPP.

Construction memory or time is tight: binary fuse needs about 24 bytes/key of temporary memory (2.4 GB for 100M keys), construction is single-threaded, and at 10M keys xor construction took 110-120 ns/key, against 10 ns for blocked Bloom and 40-90 ns for standard Bloom (xor paper, Table 2). Binary fuse builds more than 2x faster than xor.

You need the smallest possible filter: this header ships only 3-wise fuse (about 12.5% over the lower bound). The 4-wise variant (7.5%) exists only in C++ fastfilter_cpp (issue #69), and BuRR/ribbon filters go below 1%. For sets under about 20,000 keys, the paper says xor may even beat binary fuse on size.
You need an FPP below 1/65536 or cross-endian files: there are no 32-bit fingerprints (issues #8 and #75 are open), and serialization is native byte order only.

integration.dependencies: C standard library plus libm (binaryfusefilter.h calls log, floor and round; the CMake INTERFACE target links m)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (CMake c_std_99, Makefile -std=c99). CI uses GCC 13 and Clang 18 on Ubuntu 24.04 and MinGW-w64 GCC on Windows. It uses __uint128_t where available, __umulh on MSVC x64/ARM64, and a portable fallback otherwise.
integration.platforms: Any platform with a C99 compiler. CI covers only Linux x86-64 and Windows MinGW 32/64-bit; macOS, ARM and MSVC are not in CI. No SIMD required.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From the source, contain() takes a const pointer and there is no global mutable state, so concurrent lookups on a finished filter look safe. populate() is single-threaded and must not overlap queries on the same filter.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it replaces a Bloom or cuckoo filter only for static sets. You must supply every 64-bit key at build time, and there is no incremental add or delete.

gotchas: populate() can return false, so always check it. The source comment calls failure rarer than a cosmic ray, but issue #77 showed binary_fuse16_populate failing on 20-40% of distinct key sets at about 11,480-11,521 keys. That was fixed only in v2.2.0 (2026-09-21), so update any vendored copy made before then.

Deduplicate keys yourself. When populate() sees duplicates, it sorts and deduplicates your array in place. xor8/xor16 first waste 10 failed seeds before trying that. The qsort comparator returns (int)(a - b) on uint64 keys, which is not a consistent ordering, so this fallback cannot be relied on.

binary_fuse*_populate() returns false unless the key count equals the size passed to allocate(); despite the 'up to size' comment, that size must be exact. Sizes are uint32_t, so one filter holds under about 4 billion keys.

Serialization changed format in v2.0.0 (a Size field was added). deserialize() takes no buffer length and trusts ArrayLength from the buffer, so never feed it untrusted bytes. The README's 16-bit example also names binary_fuse8_contain/free where it means the fuse16 functions.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose this over BuRR when you want a single dependency-free C99 file and faster lookups: the binary fuse paper measured ribbon queries slower than 3-wise binary fuse. BuRR still wins clearly on space, with overhead under 1% against about 12.5%. Choose it over Prefix Filter when the set is static and you cannot require Intel AVX-512 and C++17, which the Prefix-Filter README mandates; Prefix Filter supports incremental inserts and this library does not.
verified_claims_summary: The xor paper's Table 3 benchmarks the C++ fastfilter_cpp release 1.0 code (GCC 8.1 -O3 -march=native, i7-6700 Skylake, single thread, non-inlined queries, 25% of queried keys present). At 10M keys, Xor8 took 23 ns/query at 9.8 bits/key, against 40 ns for Bloom12 (12 bits/key) and 31 ns for Cuckoo12 (12.8 bits/key); at 100M keys the figures were 32, 58 and 38 ns. The binary fuse paper (GCC 10 -O3, same i7-6700 plus an EPYC 7262) shows, in plots only, that 3-wise fuse reaches about 9 bits/key with xor-level query speed and builds more than 2x faster than xor. Neither paper benchmarked this C header; its own query benchmark prints no Bloom or cuckoo comparison, and the README sample output looks like placeholder numbers.
status_note: Actively maintained: v2.2.0 shipped 2026-09-21 with a construction-failure fix. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, as nDPI and InfiniFlow Infinity do; Pebble and Databend, named in the README, use the Go and Rust ports rather than this header.
